paragraphs.heading: What an orbital is
paragraphs.text: In quantum mechanics, an atomic orbital is a function that describes where an electron in an atom is and how it behaves like a wave. It tells how the electron's charge is spread around the nucleus, and from it you can work out the chance of finding the electron in a given region. One orbital can hold at most two electrons, each with its own spin projection, written mₛ.

paragraphs.heading: Three numbers and a letter
paragraphs.text: Each orbital is labeled by three quantum numbers: n, ℓ and m_ℓ. They match the electron's energy, its orbital angular momentum, and that angular momentum measured along a chosen axis. Orbitals with ℓ = 0, 1, 2 and 3 are called s, p, d and f, and together with n these names describe an atom's electron configuration. The letters come from early names for series of alkali metal spectral lines: sharp, principal, diffuse and fundamental. Past f the letters run on in order, g, h, i, k, skipping j because some languages do not tell "i" and "j" apart.

paragraphs.heading: Waves, not little planets
paragraphs.text: Electrons do not circle the nucleus the way a planet circles a star. Instead they exist as standing waves. The lowest energy an electron can have is like the basic note of a vibrating string, and higher energies are like its harmonics. An electron is never at one single point, though its wave function gives the chance of interacting with it at a point. Its charge acts as if smeared through space, with the amount at each spot proportional to the square of the wave function's magnitude.

paragraphs.heading: Still partly a particle
paragraphs.text: Electrons keep some particle-like traits. The number of them around a nucleus is always a whole number, and they jump between orbitals as particles do: if one photon strikes, only one electron changes state. Each wave state carries the same charge as the electron and a single spin, up or down. So an electron cannot be pictured simply as a solid ball.

paragraphs.heading: An atmosphere around a planet
paragraphs.text: One picture is a large, often oddly shaped "atmosphere", the electron, spread around a relatively tiny planet, the nucleus. Orbitals give the exact shape of this atmosphere only when the atom has a single electron. As more electrons are added, they tend to fill the space around the nucleus more evenly. The resulting electron cloud tends toward a roughly spherical zone of probability, because of the uncertainty principle.

paragraphs.heading: Mixtures of states
paragraphs.text: The orbital states described so far are eigenstates, and for each eigenstate a property has a value called an eigenvalue. A real electron exists as a superposition, a blend of states that resembles a weighted average but with complex numbers as the weights. For example, a mix of the states (2, 1, 0) and (2, 1, 1) has n equal to 2 and ℓ equal to 1. Its m_ℓ, though, is not a fraction like 1/2; it is ambiguous, either exactly 0 or exactly 1. Eigenstates are used because they make the math easier.

paragraphs.heading: Orbitals and spectral lines
paragraphs.text: Atomic spectral lines come from jumps, called transitions, between an atom's quantum states. These states are usually tied to an electron configuration, a scheme of which orbitals are filled; the ground state of neon, for instance, is 1s² 2s² 2p⁶. That makes orbitals a handy way to picture a transition: an electron moves from a filled orbital to an empty one. Still, electrons are fermions, governed by the Pauli exclusion principle, and they cannot be told apart from each other.
